BUDDY DEFRANCO
NEA Jazz Master (2006)
Interviewee: Buddy DeFranco (February 17, 1923 – December 24, 2014)
Interviewer: Molly Murphy with recording engineer Ken Kimery Description: Transcript, 105 pp.
Hello, I’m Molly Murphy and we’re sitting down here in the beautiful home of Buddy DeFranco in Panama City, Florida. It is November 8th, 2008. Hello Buddy.
It’s outrageous.
[laughs]
I protest.
I would like to begin this session by having you state your very impressive name, which is worthy of Italian nobility.

Right. Well, I can’t really say it in Italian. I used to speak Italian fairly well, but it’s so bad now that I’m almost ashamed. But in Italian it would be Bonifacio, my first name; Bonifacio – Ferdinando – Leonardo. Am I getting close? DeFranco.
And you’re the only one, probably, who can say that because I’ve asked so many other people – what’s his real name?
Real name, yeah.
And people take the wildest stabs and they always get it wrong.

Yeah the trouble is that, I’m Buddy because it’s when I went to school, first went to school; the teacher would look at my name and say “Bonli, Bonie, Boni- Forborni, Borni.” And all the kids would giggle and laugh and I’d be embarrassed. So it
wasn’t long before my family finally said, “Buddy.” Buddy, lets keep it Buddy. We don’t need all that.
Smart. And you, can you tell us your date of birth and where you were born?
I will not. [laughs]
[laughs] Don’t be vain now. DeFranco; Don’t be vain.
We’re documenting.
That’s all I have left is vain. Let me see, February 17th, 1923.
And you were born in?

I was born in Camden, New Jersey on Van Hook Street, I don’t know if it’s still there. And, but, shortly after, a few years, a couple years after that my family moved to Philadelphia. And I was kind of raised in south Philadelphia from that point on, until I left to go on the road.
And Philly was a place where lots of jazz musicians lived but…
Oh, many good musicians.
I think a lot of them, like you, maybe kind of migrated there, right? Is that right? The Heath brothers and Coltrane, they weren’t actually born there, but they.
Coltrane, Dizzy, yep. Who am I thinking of now? That’s terrible. My memory is not what it used to be. But Benny Golson and uh…
Joe Wilder.

Joe Wilder, of course, we were in the same class together. Red Rodney. In face, Red, when I was going to this music school, well it was a vocational school; it had a terrific music course. My last term there was when Red Rodney came in. I remember him coming into it.
And, of course, Joe Wilder was there with you.
Oh Joe, Joe and I were classmates for a couple years.
Ok, but that’s skipping ahead a little bit. Lets first talk a little bit about your family because you endured a lot of hardship as a kid, you know, in your family.

Well, I didn’t really endure that much hardship when you think about. From the standpoint if you observed my life, you would say “yes.” But my brother and I, Leonard, older brother, he and I kind of palled around. A great example was my father was blind, he lost his sight when I was about a year or two years old, I can’t remember exactly. And that was devastating for him.
And how did he lose it again? Just some accident?

It was an industrial accident. He was a foreman of a, in some factory, and he got some infection in his eye. And it was terrible circumstances, he had, he got this infection that was pretty serious, and the doctor said, “Well, this is so bad you’ve got to go into the hospital and maybe we’ll take that eye out and we’ll save the other one. And he went into the hospital and the doctor that was supposed to operate on him was in an auto accident and he couldn’t communicate with the hospital well enough. The nurses kind of messed up a little bit. And he lay in the hospital for a couple days and the infection spread to both eyes. And so he had to have both eyes removed.
Oh my God.
Yeah. Can you imagine the shock?
No.

And he didn’t talk about that for years. Years and years, he wouldn’t say. But one time we had a really serious talk about life and all that. And he told me about the first year of his life he would dream that he could see and then wake up to the realization that he couldn’t. Everyday, he said, for a year every day he just, you know, it tore him up. And then one day he said to himself, “Well, this is it, if I’m not dead and I’m going to live this way, I’ve got to figure out what to do.” And he did.
How old was he when that happened?
Boy. You know, I don’t know. Embarrassing, but I don’t really know. But a young man, of course.
But you were a kid when it happened?

Yeah, sure. I was about two I guess, or something. And then he had three more children, they had. When I say, “he had”, my mom and he had three more children. And uh, depression time. No money, I mean no money. But my brother and I always seemed to have fun. Whatever it was, we made airplane models or we’d find boxes and made a skate-mobile or something. And finally found music, both of us found music, of course.
And this is your brother Leonard?
Leonard, yeah.
And was he a year older than you?

He was a year older, yeah. And he played guitar and I played mandolin. And it was an enjoyable time for us, in a sense. We were never aware of the real bad circumstances that we were living in. And a good example was, my dad would try several things in order to make a living and my mom was a very bright lady, but very frail and, in fact, she lost it. She had to be put away in a state hospital because five children, blind husband, and no money. Figure that one.
And didn’t your youngest, didn’t her youngest child die?

Yeah, the youngest child, Freddy, died in a hospital, yeah. From, really from a lot of things, malnutrition among others. But my dad would do several things and he was going to school to try to learn—he went to the School for the Blind in Overbrook, Pennsylvania—trying to learn piano tuning and repairing and he became an expert piano technician. But during the interim he would do certain things and he had this candy route. He would sell these cheeky candy bars and my brother and I would take turns taking him around the whole city where he would service these vendor machines. And sometimes when he didn’t have enough money for a dinner or something or food, he would give us a candy bar. Well, my brother and I were elated, we got a candy bar for dinner, that was fantastic, you know. So in that way I said we never really felt that terrible poverty. They did, of course, my parents really had a terrible time of it.
Do you remember when your mother was institutionalized? You were, hold old were you? You were eight?
Oh yeah, I remember pretty well.
You do?

Yeah, and she, she didn’t know, she was torn between a religion, which was Catholic, and she and my dad went to the priest. The doctor told her not to have any more children; it was bad for her. But the priest said, “That’s ridiculous, you can always find some milk for your child, you will always provide for your child, God will.” Well I don’t know, somehow it didn’t work out that way. She was torn between eliminating her children and herself from, and my dad would not have the burden, such a burden. And he would stay awake at night, sometimes all night long, because she would walk around the house with a knife thinking about, you know, maybe getting rid of her children and herself because of the impossible situation. It even pains me to speak about it I guess.
I can imagine.
But that, you know. When people talk about life and its tribulations and worry about some trivial things. When you think about my parents, incredible. Just, and
how they survived, well especially my dad survived really. He got to be the president of the Blind Federation of Pennsylvania chapter and did fairly well as a piano technician.

I just have to interject and point out the absurdity of when I first brought this up and suggest that you endured some hardship in your [laughs] childhood and you said, “No.” And then followed it with yeah, that’s Buddy DeFranco in a nutshell.

You know, well, [laughs] it’s just my observations and my feelings, you know. Well, when you think about it, when we were just kids, it was really fun to find wood or different things to make a skate-mobile or to make an airplane model and watch it fly, it’s great, that’s fun. And we got, my dad had a mandolin and we learned to play that.
So that was your first instrument?
Yeah.
You started at age? What? Five?
Five. About five.
And you started because you had a mandolin in the house? Is that why?

Yeah, and my brother played guitar. We used to play sometimes, sometimes we’d play a duet in school. One time a little girl announced us, “Buddy DeFranco” – no Bonafici she said it, it wasn’t Buddy at the time – “Bonafici Franco will play a mandolin solo occupied by his brother [laughs] on the guitar, I remember that.
[laughs] That’s very cute.
And then I went to the clarinet after that.
So your dad, his interest in becoming a piano tuner, he was obviously already had a lot of musical interest. He played instruments and was an amateur.
Oh yeah, yes. In fact, the whole family did, my granddad, grandmother. Music was always the focal point of our entertainment.
And were you growing up hearing a lot of recordings?

A lot of recordings, and in those days the big bands started recording, Ellington and Benny Goodman, and all those people. And the opera was, very you know, naturally, that permeated especially with my granddad, he loved the opera.
Italian life.
One time he sent my brother and I to the opera, you know, to be exposed to the “civilized music” as he said. “Real music, not that stuff you listen.” And we went to the opera and we came back.
Do you remember what it was?
No. I can’t remember what the opera was. It must have been an Italian opera, you know, probably Verdi. And he said, “How did you like it.” We said, “It would be great without the singing.”
[laughs]
What we did was we, we meant that, you know, the opera, the singing was ok and all that. But that the marvelous music from the orchestra…
So it was the instrumental…
The instrumental music was great, yeah. That really impressed us.
Forget the singing, forget the plot.
Yeah, well, yeah the plot. You know is…
They’re always kind of silly and tragic. [laughter]
Yeah. Yeah, that was another thing where we learned what the plots were and what they were saying over and over again. It didn’t make any sense, you know, it was boring.
So you mentioned your grandfather, so had he, had your grandparents come from Italy?
They came from Italy, yeah.
So they were Italian?
Yeah, they were Italian.
Were they speaking mostly Italian?

Yeah, mostly, well they made a really a valiant attempt to speak English. It wound up that Italian broken English was really a comedy to listen to them. I loved it. But they were determined to be American. And they wanted us to be American; they wanted my dad to be American, to speak English. It was kind of funny, they could have had, they had as Italians they had great words about different things that apply in English. For instance, one funny situation was that we had at, my grandfather had at his home in

south Philadelphia, in the back was a typical outhouse. There was no bathroom inside, a toilet really, inside the home. But it was outside. And of course I had to in wintertime, summertime, every time to the back. And he used to call that “backhowsa.” [sic] Backhouse. And it became “backhowsit.” [sic] Backhowsit that. So my brother and I adopted that as Italian and for years I went through Italy asking people where the “backhowsit” was and nobody knew what I was talking about. And Frank Tiberi would let it go, we were together and he’d break up and let it go, and he’d let me get caught in that trap every time. He thought that was hilarious. Until one time he told me, “You know, Buddy, that’s not a word.” [laughter]
[laughter] That’s funny. Yeah, I read somewhere where you were quoting your grandfather or something, as saying something about a “Your picture in the paper” [accented] or, heavy accent, clearly.
Oh yeah. Yeah, “Your picture in the paper.” [accented] “What have you got in your pocket? he says. [accented]
So did they live in Philly with you?

Well, as it turned out my father had married twice, he had gotten a divorce from my mom. The one thing, they went through, unbelievable, the third act of Faust to get a divorce, you know. It was ridiculous what he had to go through because, there again, the family physician said that he should have a mother for us you know, somebody with him. So he got married to this lady and it didn’t work out at all. But in the interim my aunts, both Grace and Lucy, and my uncle there, Anthony, took care of us. And we moved to…
Were they you dad’s siblings?
Hm?
Were they you dad’s siblings?
Yeah, my father’s siblings. My aunt Grace was really surrogate mother for many years. She was great.
Yeah, I would have to imagine. If you essentially lost your mom when you were eight, that means your older brother was nine and then there were three others who were even younger than that, so…
Yep, sister younger and another younger brother, and then another younger brother yet after that.
Were you guys taking care of the younger ones much, you and your brother?
Oh yeah, and…
Because if your dad is out trying to make a living…
My aunt Grace took the responsibility of the four of us and she was like our mother for many years, many years.
Well, more about the musical environment around you. Your dad played in a group, correct?
Oh yeah, he played in a group.
And the name was?

They were all blind, a blind group. The name of the group was the Jovial Night Owls. Isn’t that great? Jovial Night Owls. And they played, the style of their band was like the Mummers parade bands in Philadelphia on a New Year’s Day when these bands would, Mummers parade bands would go all the way up Broad Street and play this specific sound. In fact, a band leader by the name of Art Mooney copped that style and made a big recording of I’m Looking Over a Four-leaf Clover. That was the style of the Mummers parade; well the Jovial Night Owls had that style of playing. And once in awhile they would invite my brother and I to sit in and play along with them. That’s kind of where it started, where we started playing with groups and sitting in.
So by then you had picked up clarinet. Why don’t you talk a little bit about…
Oh yeah…
…looking at, I know you were more interested in saxophone at first.

…I was at first. But then an itinerant musician, Virgil Cotrill, we used to call him “Happy.” “Happy Cotrill” was living in the neighborhood and he was my first clarinet teacher, but he said I should play clarinet first and not saxophone because if you play clarinet first the sax will come easier. If you turn it around and play sax first, clarinet is much more difficult. So he taught me for over a year. Started me out playing all the…

And this is when you are eight, eight years old? DeFranco:…about eight years old, yeah. Seven years old, something like that. And then he left town, he was playing with some local bands in Philadelphia. Strangest thing was many, many years later, just maybe about fifteen years ago, suddenly Happy Cotrill appears. He was living in Wilmington, North Carolina.
Yeah, I read that. That’s the strangest story. Tell that story. How did that happen again, you?

Yeah, well. Its really a convoluted story. I had a furniture manufacturer who was interested in a pianist. His name escapes me. Do you remember the pianist’s name? I can’t remember his name. Oh that’s terrible. That’s why I hate these interviews. Good bye. [laughter]
[laughter] Well, it was good while it lasted.

Anyway, we talked about this young pianist, and we played and met him, he was a good player, and we played together. And he said, “You know, we know a saxophone/clarinet player, he’s retired now, but he said that he taught you.” And I said, “Well, how could that be?” He said, “Yeah, his name was Cotrill.” I said, “Whoa, Happy Cotrill.” After seventy years, or sixty years, whatever it is, I don’t know. But we got together, I got some pictures of us together, yeah.
That must have been amazing.
Isn’t that incredible?
Had he followed your career?
Through the years he said yeah he did, from time to time, yeah.
You must have been his claim to fame. [laughter]
In a way, in a way.
Downbeat poll after Downbeat poll.

Right, right. And then after that, I was playing in, I was living in my aunt’s house. And one Sunday I was practicing, I always practice. I used to practice day and night, and the neighbors really got fed up with that. I think one time, I’m pretty sure, they got a petition against my practicing, so I had to limit that to eight hours a day.
This was when you were just a little kid?
Yeah. Yeah. Oh I loved to practice, yeah, I really enjoyed it.
That’s pretty unusual for someone that young.
Yes! It was fascinating!
And what were you practicing? How did you practice?

The fundamentals. I wanted to be what they called in those days, they still do call, legitimate. Legitimate clarinet player, as opposed to if you played jazz your were illegitimate, you know. A fellow of by the name of William D. Simone lived a few blocks

away from, he was walking by. He was a clarinetist who played in the Earl Theatre in Philadelphia, played in the pit, played sax and clarinet. He banged on the door and said, “I heard the clarinet, and I hear this kid playing.” He said, “ I think he has potential.”
Wow.

Willy D. Simone was his name and he taught me for quite a few years. For about a year and a half for nothing, didn’t take any money. As years went on I began to play jobs and make a few dollars, sometimes three or four, five dollars a job. And Willy said, “Ok, you’re working now you have a dollar a lesson.” So I paid him a dollar a lesson. But he really set me in the right direction for being a clarinetist because he insisted on me being a well-schooled musician, and a well-schooled clarinetist. And he was by himself; he was a great clarinet player.
And was he, what kind of repertoire was he having you practice?

Well he played in the pit in the Earl Theatre and it was everything. He played for the shows, and for the dancers, for singers, for comedians, for opera singers and he was well schooled in the symphonic area. So he taught me the correct way to play the clarinet. Fingering techniques and all that and gave me the right books to study. And he was also interested in jazz, of course. In those days he loved Benny Goodman and Artie Shaw. So he would try to emulate their playing and that’s how I kind of got interested in jazz clarinet. I heard…
So he was one of the people kind of directing you to those performers.

Oh yeah, yeah. And then in the Earl Theatre they had these stage shows. Four and five shows a day. Big bands were coming through, and they’d have a big band and a movie. The big band for an hour and then they’d run a movie and a newsreel, and then the band would come play another show. I remember listening to Tommy Dorsey, watching and listening to Tommy Dorsey’s band. He featured a clarinetist, Johnny Mintz. Johnny played a long solo and I was so impressed, that kind of tipped me over into the area of jazz. I wanted to be a jazz clarinetist from that point on. Then I heard Benny Goodman, of course, everyone did, and he was a giant. And then I heard Artie Shaw, and Artie Shaw really was…
So how old were you when you heard Johnny Mintz? And that was live, that was a live performance.

That was live. I must have been nine, ten years old. Of course, Artie Shaw became my favorite for a long, he still is one of my favorites. They were both; Benny Goodman and Artie were both marvelous players.
Do you remember specific recordings that you were listening to of them? I mean, did you go out and buy records or was that hard to come by?

Yeah, no we could, we went and bought some records, a 78-rpm records. And, of course, I listened to the obvious ones, you know. Benny’s Don’t Be That Way, and Let’s Dance, and Goodbye, and Artie’s Stardust. Moonglow. I could, in those days I used to play his solos.
Did you play along with the music?
Yeah, I’d play along with the records and sometimes it was rough because, many times, a turntable wouldn’t be in tune with what you were doing…
[laughter] Also clarinet, so…
You’d have to worry about fabricating something in between. But I got through that way, it was a good way to learn.

So, I mean, that’s a pretty young age to be listening to people and really absorbing things stylistically. But at that age, what about each of those players’ styles was interesting to you. Between Johnny Mintz, and Benny Goodman, and Artie Shaw. What did you like about them?

Lets see. Johnny Mintz was a self-taught clarinetist that had a fascinating technique on the instrument and he could play fast. He had a great technique. Benny Goodman also had exceptional technique on the instrument. And he could also, had that swing lilt. He was known as the King of Swing, he had that swing lilt in his playing. Artie was different. Artie was different, Artie was like, played the clarinet like a fine violinist. It was more melodic, and extended his harmonic development was much more interesting and extended than Benny Goodman, or Johnny Mintz at that time. And, of course, as a clarinet playing jazz he took more “chances” as we say on the instrument and got away with it, got through with it. He kind of influenced me up until I heard Bird and that was…
All bets were off.
Wow, it was a complete change in my approach and everything. It all augured well for that, to go into that bebop area.
Getting back to Tommy Dorsey. He came back into your life in the form of the Tommy Dorsey Swing Contest.
Yeah, that was 1938 I think.
1930-yeah, it was.

I think. He was going through the country. It was called Tommy Dorsey Swing Contest. Management, they were holding auditions. I learned from Charlie Ventura, who lived in my neighborhood, we used to play together that they were
auditioning for the Dorsey contest. So I went up and auditioned and got through the audition, there were four contestants. I won that night. It was broadcast nationwide.
Backed by the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra.
Backed by the band, yeah.
That’s amazing! So hold old were you?
Yeah, fourteen, thirteen, in my teens, early teens
And this is where Willy D. Simone, didn’t he orchestrate some sort of…[laughter]

Well, yeah. The whole thing was unfair in a way because I was a pretty good clarinet for being pretty bad, you know, one of those things. Willy said to me, “You’re going to win that contest. I’m going to make sure you win that contest. And so you have to not wear the long pants you just got you, you have to wear knickers.” And he said, “People will love it, because you’ll look that much younger, wear knickers and…”
So that’s about the age that boys moved into long pants?
Moved into long pants, sure…
Thirteen? Fourteen? DeFranco:…I was so proud of them, you know, so happy.
So that must have been humiliating to…[laughter]

It was humiliating. And then he said, “You’re going to play Honeysuckle Rose, everybody likes that song.” At the end of the song he showed me how to hold up the clarinet up with one hand, one hand and play one note, and poke that one note through. He said, “Hold your hand out so that the people will see you’re playing with one.” He said, “You’ll break it up!” And to me that was really, even at that time, that was dumb, corny stuff, you know, ridiculous. But I did it and he was in the pit and he was giving me directions from the pit. And I finally got through the whole thing and it was an abominable solo, but the people, I mean those other contestants didn’t have a chance. You know, here’s a kid with a clarinet almost as tall as he was.
How did they make the decision who won? Was it audience reaction?
They have, yeah, audience applause. The had one of those…
Applause-o-meters.

Applause meters. [laughter] Oh yea, they had a pretty good trumpet player, who was a cadet. And a vibes player was quite good. And I believe a trombone player and myself. Of course, the other guys were pretty good, but it didn’t mean anything, you know, they didn’t have a chance.
Were you nervous?
Yeah, of course…
Having this big broadcast live, nationally?
Yeah, scared to death…
Terrifying. DeFranco:…but I got through it.
Do I remember that someone did record that…
Yeah, somebody had taken a… Murphy:…broadcast? Is there a recording?

Yeah, somebody had take a recording, they had this old recording machine, these vinyl machines that, it wasn’t a wire, it was a vinyl machine that they recorded on. It was kind of distorted, I heard it.
Do you have it?
No! Thank goodness. [laughter]
Darn it! [laughter]
I’m not being modest, it was pretty bad. It was pretty bad. [laughter]
Well, it certainly propelled you into a lot of…
Yeah… Murphy:…other stuff. DeFranco:…and on that show Tommy said, “Stick around kid, you’re going to play in my band someday.” That was another round of applause I got.
How often do you think he said that?
Not very often really. And the amazing thing was that I did, I did play with Tommy Dorsey many years later, and he remembered that, you know, of course.
Even less often that it would actually come to fruition, that’s amazing.

Typical of Dorsey. He was an interesting person, he was a marvelous trombonist, one of the best I ever heard. Strict band leader. But he was bigger than life, it was frightening, very intimidating. I sat down even to audition for his big band many years later. I had played Charlie Barnet and Gene Krupa, and Ted Fiorito, and a few other bands, territory bands. I sat down and they had these chairs lined up for the sax section, and a rhythm there section set up. And in came a pianist, I forgot his name now, anyway. Gene Krupa was playing drums. Gene had just got out of jail and Tommy hired him. And Sandy Block came in on bass. And the sax section lined up with the empty chair, and I sat in the chair. And then Tommy Dorsey came in with his entourage, three or four people, and management. I think he had his wife with him, Pat Dane, who was strange! Beautiful lady, but in terrifying ways. And he came up to me, and you know, I guess. Giant, he looked like he was ten feet tall, and I’m sitting there with a clarinet and sax. And then Sy Oliver came over and he told me what songs to get out, and they picked the toughest songs to play. And Tommy said, “You remember kid, I told you you’d play in my band someday, right?” I grinned, I said, “Yeah.” He said, “Well, don’t think you’ve got it made, because if you blow this you’re out of here.” [laughter] For starters, I didn’t even play a note.
That’s amazing that he remembered. Did someone tip him off do you think?
Oh yeah, he remembered.
Or do you think he just remembered?
Yeah, he remembered…
Very impressive. DeFranco:…Well, he had that kind of a memory anyway, I learned that.
You know, I wanted to ask you about that performance. Had you ever played with a full orchestra before? I mean a big band?
Oh, sure.
You had?

Yeah, because at the time we were, when I say we it was, Al Alberts played piano. He was the, originated that group, I forgot the name of the group, anyway. Four Aces, the Four Aces. They were very popular in those days. He played piano in the band,
and we were all kids, and Joe Wilder was in the band occasionally. And we had this big band and we’d play different block parties around south Philadelphia.
Is this the BandBusters?
This was the BandBusters and we played every Sunday morning on the “Horn and Hardart Children’s Hour” with a big band.
So, maybe to go back. That’s right. So was this when you were at the Massbaum school?
Yeah, we were going to Massbaum.
Ok, so just to back up a tiny bit. You, instead of going to regular old high school, you went to a vocational high school.

Right. We learned about this music course that they had up in north Philadelphia. I had decided, and my dad at the time, made the decision that I should go up there. It was a vocational school, great music course and great teachers. There again, luck was in my corner because Myra Lavin was a band and orchestra conductor. And Ross Wyre had the band, the concert band. They were both great teachers and Mira Lavin especially was terrific. There I got real excellent schooling in the classical field playing in his orchestra.
Did you have to audition in order to get into that school?
Yeah, oh yeah. You had to audition, to play different things. But that was some of the best training I ever had.
And all, so-called legit…
Legit, yeah. Murphy:…what was their attitude about jazz?

Oh, they liked jazz. But they insisted that if we’re going to have what they called a big band, stage band, that we would have to play in the orchestra and concert band. If we couldn’t cut the orchestra or concert band, then we could have a big band, swing band. We had a good band, a lot of good players in there.

I’m remembering Joe Wilder making a, telling me something about that school, that in the orchestra you weren’t supposed to be playing jazz repertoire and somebody would sneak in a flatted fifth. And everybody would stop and the director would say, “Who played flatted fifth?” [laughter]
Or more likely he knew who played it and throw his baton in that direction. Mr. Lavin had ears like an elephant.
So while you were there that’s when you got this band together, the BandBusters. And how many people?
Yeah, Elliot Lawrence was in that band playing tenor sax. And his dad was the MC and he owned the radio station that we played in every Sunday morning. About fourteen, fifteen guys in the band.
And was there a leader?
Well, my brother and I were kind of leaders, but there was no real leader as such. So it was the BandBusters featuring Leonard and Buddy and Elliot Lawrence. Pretty good band by all standards.
And so you were playing on Sunday mornings, did you play gigs, too?
Hm?
Did you played hired gigs, too?
Yeah, we played some gigs, yeah.
You did. I think I read, there must have been a clipping from the newspaper, an interview with you, and the slang, the terminology you used was just hilarious. [laughter]
Yeah, although that was, we didn’t use that much swing jazz terminology as was put in the paper. The guy that wrote it up…
You mean they made that up?
Hm?
He made it up?
Yeah, he made a lot of it up, yeah, you know.
Your licorice stick?
Yeah, licorice stick.

Well, where do we start? First of all, the clarinet is really not an octave instrument, in other words, as opposed to say the saxophone. If you play one scale on the saxophone and you depress and octave key, that’s what you’ll get higher, one octave higher. So the fingering stays essentially the same from one octave to the next. The pads cover the holes; you depress the pads, cover the holes. On the clarinet you’ve got six holes that are open and three, actually seven, depends on the clarinet that you are playing, seven holes that are open, or six holes that are open. But you have to close those holes with your fingers. If you just, fingers stray a little bit from closing those holes you’ll get a squeak or the note won’t come out. Plus the fact that there’s no octave key, they call it an octave key on the clarinet but really it’s a register key. So if you play one note and you depress that key as you would on a saxophone, you don’t get an octave higher, you get a twelfth higher. Then you come into the middle register of the clarinet, which is the most difficult, the left hand, and you get a completely different set of fingerings for the same notes an octave lower, different set of fingerings. Then into the next one, which is not an octave higher, it’s a twelfth higher, and you go up to that top of that, say, that scale and then you get from that point up to the highest register a completely different set of
fingerings again. So you’re dealing with four sets of fingerings to play all these notes on the clarinet.

Both ears? DeFranco:…tinnitus. I live with that, sure. But I’ve learned to put it in the background. And I’m fortunate it that it’s not a note, there’s not a note there involved. I think maybe if it was a note or two notes it might be problematic, but it’s not, it’s a hiss. It’s always there, but I’ve learned to shove that in the background and play.
Nobody knows what causes it; nobody knows how to get rid of it?
No, not really, I’ve tried everything, I’ve spoken to a lot of doctors. They really don’t, there’s no cure for that. And sometimes the hiss is louder than the band I’m

working with, sometimes, you know, it gets old, but not that often. And I spoke to one doctor some years ago who was pretty familiar with music and jazz and he said, “Who was your drummer?” [laughter]
[laughter]

And I said, “Art Blakey.” And he said, “Go get him. He’s the guy.” And you know he might be right because I realize now that for many years I’d stand and play in front of the drummer. I shouldn’t have, but I did. I might have like the idea of the beat and the feeling if he’s a good drummer, I liked, you know. Stand in front of Jeff Hamilton or somebody like that, or even those days Art Blakey. But I shouldn’t have because the sound of the drums and the cymbals, they wash over you. And it might have started that. Also, many years ago with my cousin I went, Joyce and I went to, fountain in the woods and I shot of some pistols and one shot from a twenty-two did something to my ear.
Wow.
But then it went away and then all of a sudden it started coming back, that ringing.
You know Rudy Van Gelder won’t wear headphones ever because he’s worried about what that might do to his hearing.
I think it could, he might be right, yeah.
Which, I mean you think of a recording engineer, I think of…
That’s what they do. Murphy:…that’s all, you know, that is the vision of a recording engineer, but he said he hasn’t worn headphones for, I don’t know, thirty years.
Well, he’s proved that you don’t need them, eh?
Yep.
He’s done a great job.
And one other thing that you had a problem with was trigger finger. What is?
Yeah, this finger, trigger finger, it still clicks a little bit.
What happens, does it get, it just gets locked into place?
I got a, yeah, sometimes I’d wake up and it would be locked and I’d have to pull it out. I got an injection of cortisone--wasn’t it cortisone—yeah, cortisone and in a

few weeks it went away. Even now I wake up and it sticks a little bit but then after a short while it’s gone, so that worked out ok. I’m fighting the battle now with this jaw and my eyes, and I have double vision.
Double vision?

Double vision, that’s why I wear these glasses, they have prisms on both sides to bring my eyes in focus, closer together. Its been seriously bad the past few weeks but I’ve got these glasses and they may help train my eyes because now I see both of you.
[laughter]
[laughter] I hope they look good.
How are you both? [humorously] So that’s kind of a problem except that in a sick way I always say, “If I read music I can play twice as fast.” [laughter]
Right. [laughter] Well, that’s tough. “Getting old is not for the weak,” someone once told me.

It’s ridiculous, it really is ridiculous. Who ever made that thing up; it doesn’t make any sense. I hate to blame it on God—what do I know about God, you know—but it doesn’t make any sense. You’re supposed to really get better over the years; stronger and better.
Wiser.
[laughter] Wiser. Yeah, there we go again, when you’re young you know it all, you know everything, and that diminishes to the point that you’re really frustrated because…
[AUDIO RECORDER STOPPED AND RESTARTED]
DeFranco:…you say to yourself, “Don’t I know anything?”
Right.
“Anything, give me something to hang onto.”
You go back to the big bang theory.
Big bang theory.
Try to figure that out.
Yeah, right.
[Background (Kimery): Here we go.]
So one thing that we haven’t really covered is your instruments and you’ve changed instruments a little bit over the years but you said not very much.

No, when I consider compared to other clarinetists, I stayed with the same instrument for many years, through the years. For instance, the first actual decent clarinet I played on was a Selmer and I kind of oscillated between that and Buffet for some years. And I got a hold of a, mainly because of Artie Shaw again, a BT—Balanced Tone Selmer—and I used that for many years. And then I did some clinic and ran into Vito Pascucci; Vito Pascucci brought the LeBlanc clarinet to the United State from France. There’s an interesting guy, he would be, it would be incredible to interview somebody like that, Vito Pascucci, because he went to France, to Paris and he was originally in the service with the Glenn Miller Orchestra, he was a technician and repaired instruments and all that, a clarinet player. And he went to Paris and befriended the LeBlanc family, although he didn’t speak French and they didn’t speak English, but somehow he convinced them that he should take some of those clarinets to the United States. And he started at his home in Kenosha, Wisconsin with a few LeBlanc clarinets. And from that point on built the LeBlanc name and clarinet in the United States to gigantic proportions. So I played, they were developing a new model of LeBlanc, which I liked, it has some better features than the ones I’d been playing, so I played LeBlanc for many years— many, many years. They sponsored a lot of clinics that I did, too, and it was easy because I liked the instrument I was playing so I could easily say here to the students, “Here’s what I play.” And over the years Yamaha came into the picture and they started developing clarinets and they brought some of their nice clarinets to the United States. After maybe thirty years, I guess, that I played LeBlanc, I’ve tried the Yamaha and I liked it very much and it had some features that mine didn’t at the time, and been playing Yamaha for maybe thirty years also, from that point on. Its funny, you know, I used to get some funny inquires about Yamaha in the very beginning because they were really not, I didn’t know this, but they were a piano company first and then they got into the vehicles and then other instruments, and they now make top line instruments, marvelous. And they managed to over the years brain pick all the top clarinetists and clarinet players and clarinet companies and they’ve put together a fine instrument. But I used to get some funny inquires about playing Yamaha in the beginning, you know, “What mileage do you get on your clarinet?” But its been thirty some years and that was it.
You know what I didn’t ask you about was your first clarinet.

My first clarinet was a strange; well my dad was poor, of course. In fact, he spent the rent money for my clarinet and my uncle wouldn’t speak to him for months because he did that; such an outrageous thing, spend rent money for a clarinet. And the clarinet was combination of a wooden top and a hard rubber bottom.
Where did he get it?

At a pawnshop, a pawnshop that dealt with musical instruments. And my teacher at the time came over and helped out and picked out an instrument. I think it was thirty dollars or some minimal amount. One time I was, I picked up, it was a hard rubber bottom to it, and I picked it up and I was shaking out the saliva, I dropped the clarinet and broke the joint on the bottom. And I tried, my brother and I tried to hide it from my father, we tried to heat this hard rubber to glue together to stick together and it wouldn’t go and what a ridiculous thing. But finally I told my dad about it and we went to a repairman and he managed to fix, to screw on a little joint part that holds the bell and I used that until we could afford a real clarinet, one whole clarinet that I think that was a Selmer. But the first one was just a strange mongrel.
Well, amazing to have, you know, a parent with such dedication…
Yeah, he was… Murphy:…when your child is that young to have some vision and actually put some hard earned money into it.

Yeah, I always appreciated it. Not only that, my dad was an unusual person, very kind man and tried his best to keep all of us somewhat stable. And I think we’re fortunate, not one of us went off the track, we still held some values and kept somewhat of a normal life, all of us, through the years.
Just for documenting purposes, what were your parents’ full names?

Leonard was my dad’s name, Leonard DeFranco, and my mom was Louise Giordano, and her family was from Calabria, her parents. My dad’s parents were from Foggia, which is kind of central Italy. I don’t know how my grandparents got together at all or where they met, but they somehow got to the United States. One of my uncles was born in Italy; he was about a year old when my grandparents came to the United States and settled by mistake in Philadelphia. They were originally going to go to New York and something went wrong and they found Philadelphia and managed to settle in South Philadelphia. So it’s a combination of Calabria—they call it Calabrese—and Foggia, Foggian.
And your mother’s parents also lived in the U.S?
My mother’s parents…
So both sets, did you grow up being close to both sets of grandparents?
No.
No.
Mostly my dad’s parents. In fact, that’s where I lived at their house for so long. Although we, you know, spent some time with my mother’s parents, but I never got to really know them.
Were they also in Philly?
No. They were in Philly for a while, but I think they went to New Jersey, but I lost track of them.
Last night you mentioned that your grandfather made wine.

He made his own wine; there again, they used to call it “Diego Red.” It was rough stuff and once a year he’d have the wine company, the grapes in boxes shoved in the bottom into the cellar from the outside from the street. And he had a couple barrels and he had a wine press, and he’d press the grapes and make this wine. Put it in the barrels and age the wine. He did a pretty good job and he made good wine, except that it was very strong. I mentioned that I got stoned, out of it on it. But that was a ritual once a year with him; he was quite a colorful character. I still, I find myself imitating him. In fact, a good friend of mine the other day said he did same thing, finding himself imitating his grandfather of all things, saying the same things.
What kinds of things?

Well, I think I mentioned before that he had funny sayings about, “What have you got in the pocket” is one. He liked Benny Goodman, my grandfather liked Benny Goodman, and every time I come back he knew that there was somehow being a comparison in the music business and he’d say to me, “Hey boy, I heard you play. Are you here Benny Good-a-one.” “What’s a matter when an will you play, you hear Benny Good-a-one he plays?” [laughter] Benny Good-a-one. And he was a funny character when it came to the religion too; I guess I followed in his footsteps. He was not antireligious but there was a portion of the whole religious experience that he simply wouldn’t accept, and I followed suit in my life. And there again, at the expense of sounding antisocial or not politically correct, the priests in those days they worked on getting as much money as they could from this poor people in the neighborhood and they would come for collections before Christmas, before Easter, they would come to the house for the annual, or whatever it is, collections. And they would come in and my aunt would greet them, the priest, and my grandfather would be in the kitchen and he knew that the priest was in the living room and he’d yell at the top of his lungs, “Go to work like I work! Get a job! What do you come for money; we don’t have money to give you, got to work, get a job! You’re driving a car, I don’t drive a car!” And she would, my aunt would say, “Don’t pay attention to him he doesn’t know what he’s saying.” And my grandfather says, “I know what I’m saying!” Which was hilarious, you know.

But I kind of got some of that attitude generally toward religion, organized religion, from him I guess, its comical but so much truth in it. And of course, the crushing thing with my parents when the priest wouldn’t accept the fact that my mom should not have another child, they wouldn’t accept it, and to me that was so stubborn and so wrong. She was so Catholic that she did whatever the priest said, that was it that was law. That soured me on religion from that point on.
How long did she live?
She lived in her forties, in her late forties, I guess, maybe early fifties, but I don’t think.
So did you see her after?

We used to go and see her, and when I say we, my aunt would take my brother and I out to Byberry in the state hospital. She didn’t know us; she didn’t know anyone or anything and sometimes we would sit there for two hours while she stared into space not acknowledging anyone or anything. She was completely oblivious to anything happening.
Was she medicated? Do you think that?

No, not so much, it was her condition she was schizophrenic and withdrawn. She just totally blocked out the world and it was so hard and there were some incidents there that would be funny if I weren’t so tragic, it would make a great movie because one time my uncle came, my uncle Anthony. He was quite a guy he lived into his late nineties, mid-nineties, or ninety-six anyway. A veteran, a World War One veteran, and an unbelievable strength; walked through his nineties he would walk miles and fast, we never could walk with him. All of us, we’d walk with him and have to run to catch up, he was incredible he had so much strength through the years and a quick mind, a great mind. We went to see my mother one time and she was just sitting there staring, and my two aunts were with us, and my uncle, and then we noticed a lady across the way at another table and chair looking at my uncle really seriously, I mean, she started mumbling and looking at him. I said to my uncle, “Don’t look now but I think we got company, you know.” My uncle said, “Yeah, I noticed, I noticed.” And she was eating some kind of pudding or something. And then all of a sudden [spit noise] my uncle got it right in the face. [laughter] He said, “I knew it, I knew it.” Which is ridiculous, you know, but that, I don’t know who she thought he was, but he was not welcome.
She did not like him.
That was a terrible tragic segment of my life because the state hospitals were so horrible.
Yeah.

And they had so few people to take care of them and naturally the people that supposedly to take care of them were not competent really, and they would do outrageous things. They would tie them to the radiator heater to make them behave, you know, because they were out of hand a lot of them.
Right.

There again, what could they do? They didn’t have the necessary medication, which just started kind of later through my life, that they had the right medication to settle them down and treat them. Some of them got out of hand and those poor people had a lot of people on their hands to try to keep in shape, to keep in order. They resorted to a lot of nasty things.
You know, I really think as a young person you dealt with a lot of things that, you know, many people never even experience in life, even adults…
Oh, yeah.
And that’s a lot for a kid to take on.

I think it is, it does two things; it does affect you in many ways adversely, but also you learn a lot. You have practical learning life experiences and if you’re smart enough you can make some sense out of what happened. There again, you can learn to understand a lot of points of view and a lot of different people and reasoning for what they do. My point in time, I mean, I always say that a lot of people are impatient with people who are stupid. But if somebody is really stupid, can they help it? That is a fact. What can they do? That’s the way it is, that’s their concept. You can try to change them but it’s to no avail, so the next thing is to try to accept them to some degree. A lot of times in the music business we have, the situation is that there are a lot of guys, a lot of musicians who are just simply not talented who are somehow making their way into the music business. Now, what do we do? When I say, “What do we do?” The ones who are professionals, sometimes they catch on, they get popular. We can’t, you know, we can’t be going out and be revolting. You accept it, that’s it, that’s the way they are. Can try and change it, of course, but…

In talking about being an observer of people and, of course, not just, you know, in your childhood, but just encountering so many different audiences and traveling around the world, being on the road. One thing we haven’t talked about is how you relate to your audiences. Is that important to you? When you’re performing, are you aware of your audience and do they give you…

Oh, yeah, I’m aware of the audience. But in essence I really perform to the musicians that are out there. I zero in on the musicians because I know there is an immediate connection. If you make that connection the rest follows in and kind of develops and becomes a reaction from the people who really don’t know what you’re

doing and you see it, you can almost see it, it’s almost obvious at times. If there are a group of musicians who hear you and they start applauding “Yeah!” You can see the people around them say, “Well, he says, yeah, ok, this guy is good.” Although, you know they don’t really know what you’re doing, but they do react, they do react. So I try to play for the musician first, might sound idiotic but it works.
How about when you’re in a studio recording an album?

You still play for the musician; you play for the guys you’re working with and you play for the musician whose not there. That gives you some confidence and you know that you’re playing to somebody that can relate to what you’re doing. Naturally what you play, you have to also impart a feeling, rhythmic or otherwise, a feeling. [phone rings in background] That’s ok.
Little pause. Well, you have been accused of emphasizing content throughout your career over commerciality and do you ever have any regrets about following that path?

Sure, only because you know that if you deliberately gravitated toward the commercial part of anything that you do that you’re going to be more successful in terms of money. You want to get more money and you’re going to be able to get more things and all that stuff. So in that way sometimes I considered it’s unfair to my family to not be really commercial. But I feel also that if we get through and have a comfortable life, and Joyce has been great because she’s been able to help with our living to a great extent, so we are comfortable. But I regret many times that I can’t be like a lot of people who are gung ho for the commercial aspects in order to make it, to achieve stardom, or whatever that is.
And when you say you can’t be it just isn’t in your bones.
It’s not there, no, I’d be a big hypocrite. It just isn’t there.
What do you think about the state of jazz and jazz education today?

It’s in pretty fairly healthy condition by comparison, say by comparing twenty or thirty years ago, it was almost nonexistent, almost. But there again, all those band directors through the years that kept at the big band and jazz as an important part of our lives and as an American art form helped us all survive, and so it grew. Now I hear more really good jazz players, young jazz players, than ever before not only in the United States but all over the world. In other countries you hear guys who are great players, great players.
Who are some of the clarinetists that you are following? You mentioned Anat Cohen?

Anat Cohen is an excellent player, yes, and Paquito D’Rivera, and Eddie Daniels, and Ronnie Aldrich, and Ken Peplowski. There are a lot of guys and girls who are playing well, as opposed to say thirty-five years they were not known. That goes for all the instruments; there are some trumpet players and drummers, and pianists that I’ve heard young guys who are excellent now, more so than before. So it’s a pretty healthy business, it’s not like the rock business or commercial business, but it’s pretty healthy.
And you sit back as the father of bebop clarinet…

The father. [laughter] Murphy:…and they all come to you. How does it feel to be in the position of being, you know, the NEA Jazz Master? And, you know, actually to attend an event, such as you attended a couple of weeks ago, where you are in New York surrounded by a lot of the statesmen of jazz. Is that something that is enjoyable?

Yeah, positively, really gratifying, you know, because no one likes to be ignored and when you are accepted like that for what you do in the business, very gratifying. And fortunately, it doesn’t make you smug, it makes you like the idea but also gives you some imponents to continue what you are doing. So it’s a good feeling to be recognized as such. And then those people that booed in Paris don’t mean a thing. Right? Who cares? Here I am.
I keep looking at your coffee cup. [laughter]
[laughter] You like it?
“Old musicians never die, they just…”
“Decompose.” [laughter]
[laughter] That’s very fitting, good. Well, thank you. Are there any other things that anybody else would like to talk about?
I can’t, I’ll probably think of a million things, you know, when we finish.
You can call it in.
I’ll call it in, yeah. Molly, thank you very much. Ken, thank you, you’re here, but you’re not in the picture.
Not in the picture. And thank you Joyce for participating and giving all these…
Yeah. Murphy:…answers to the test questions to Buddy.
Tough questions is right.
She’s not on camera, she’s not on mike, but she’s so instrumental. [laughter]
And beautiful, “Sweet-baby” I call her. [laughter]
Sweet-baby? [laughter]
Yeah.
Thanks.
[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

segments.title: Opening and the name Bonifacio Ferdinando Leonardo
segments.summary: Murphy opens the interview in Panama City; DeFranco gives his Italian birth name and explains how he became Buddy at school.

segments.title: Born in Camden, raised in South Philadelphia, and Philly's musicians
segments.summary: He gives his birth date and place, the move to Philadelphia, and names fellow Philadelphians Joe Wilder, Red Rodney and others.

segments.title: His father goes blind after a hospital infection
segments.summary: His father lost his sight to an infection and a hospital mix-up when Buddy was about two, and slowly learned to live blind.

segments.title: Depression poverty, brother Leonard, and father's candy route
segments.summary: He and Leonard played guitar and mandolin; the mother broke down, the youngest child died, and the father retrained as a piano technician and ran a candy route.

segments.title: His mother's breakdown and institutionalization
segments.summary: He recalls his mother, torn between doctor and priest, becoming dangerous and being committed when he was about eight.

segments.title: First instrument, the mandolin, and a musical household
segments.summary: He started on his father's mandolin at five, played duets with Leonard, and grew up with family music and early big-band records.

segments.title: Grandfather sends the boys to the opera
segments.summary: The grandfather sent them to hear opera; they said it would be great without the singing.

segments.title: Italian grandparents and the word 'backhowsit'
segments.summary: His grandparents' broken English and the family joke of 'backhowsit' for the outhouse.

segments.title: Aunts Grace and Lucy and uncle Anthony raise the children
segments.summary: After the divorce the father's siblings, especially Aunt Grace, took care of the children.

segments.title: His father's blind band, the Jovial Night Owls
segments.summary: His father played in a blind group in the Mummers parade band style, and the boys sat in.

segments.title: First clarinet teacher Happy Cotrill and the reunion decades later
segments.summary: Virgil 'Happy' Cotrill taught him clarinet first, and they met again after sixty years.

segments.title: Marathon practicing and lessons with Willy D. Simone
segments.summary: He practiced day and night, and Willy D. Simone of the Earle Theatre pit taught him serious clarinet and pointed him to Goodman and Shaw.

segments.title: Stage shows at the Earl Theatre and Johnny Mintz with Dorsey
segments.summary: Big bands played the Earl Theatre; hearing Dorsey's clarinetist Johnny Mintz made him want to play jazz.

segments.title: Records, playing along, and the styles of Mintz, Goodman and Shaw
segments.summary: He learned from 78s and compares Mintz, Goodman and Artie Shaw, until hearing Bird changed everything.

segments.title: Winning the Tommy Dorsey Swing Contest in knickers
segments.summary: He won a nationally broadcast Dorsey contest at about 13 or 14, coached by Simone to wear knickers and play Honeysuckle Rose one-handed.

segments.title: Dorsey's promise and the later audition for his band
segments.summary: Dorsey told him he would play in his band someday and, years later at an audition, reminded him of it.

segments.title: The BandBusters and the Horn and Hardart Children's Hour
segments.summary: As a teenager he played in a kids' big band with Al Alberts and Joe Wilder at block parties and on radio.

segments.title: Mastbaum vocational school and its legit training
segments.summary: He attended a vocational high school with a strong music course under Lavin and Ross Wyre, where jazz was tolerated alongside orchestra.

segments.title: More on the BandBusters, Elliot Lawrence and a made-up newspaper story
segments.summary: The band had about fifteen players including Elliot Lawrence; a newspaper invented swing slang for them.

segments.title: Sneaking into the Earl Theatre to hear the big bands
segments.summary: He and friends snuck in to watch Krupa, Dorsey, Ellington, Basie, Goodman and Shaw all day, and he met Teddy Wilson.

segments.title: Philadelphia after-hours clubs and being discovered by Scat Davis
segments.summary: Billy Krechmer and Nat Siegel ran after-hours clubs where he sat in; Johnnie Scat Davis offered him a road job.

segments.title: Leaving at fifteen with Johnnie Scat Davis and life on the band bus
segments.summary: He graduated early, Davis became his guardian, and he describes one-nighters on the band bus.

segments.title: Dorsey's seven shows a day and recording-ban rehearsals
segments.summary: In Milwaukee Dorsey's band played seven shows a day and rehearsed before the Petrillo recording ban.

segments.title: Pay with Scat Davis and young pianist Dodo Marmarosa
segments.summary: He earned $75 a week with Davis and met Dodo Marmarosa, who joined at fourteen.

segments.title: Gene Krupa raids the Davis band
segments.summary: Krupa raided the Davis band by telegram; Krupa was congenial compared with Dorsey.

segments.title: Charlie Barnet, playboy bandleader, and a naked party
segments.summary: Stories about Barnet's wealthy background and a wild party at his new house.

segments.title: First recordings and Dorsey calling him away from Barnet
segments.summary: He made no solos with Barnet; his first real solo recording was Opus One with Dorsey, who called him in 1943.

segments.title: Dorsey confronts them in the train dining car
segments.summary: Marmarosa and DeFranco had gone to great expense to make a job, and Dorsey gave them a raise.

segments.title: Recordings and V-Discs with the Dorsey band
segments.summary: They discuss how many records he made with Dorsey and the V-Discs with the Dorsey trio.

segments.title: Hearing Charlie Parker with Charlie Shavers
segments.summary: Shavers took him to hear a saxophonist in Harlem on a borrowed horn, and it changed his approach to jazz.

segments.title: Why bebop is so hard on clarinet
segments.summary: He explains the clarinet's fingering problems, why Goodman and Shaw failed at bebop, and how he studied Parker.

segments.title: Meeting and playing with Parker; All the Things You Are in D
segments.summary: They first played together at a New York club, and Parker switched keys on him to teach a lesson.

segments.title: His first Metronome All-Stars session in 1946
segments.summary: He replaced Benny Goodman on the first All-Stars date alongside Parker and Gillespie.

segments.title: Avoiding drugs, and how drink and dope affected Parker and Tatum
segments.summary: He avoided needles and heavy drink, and says Parker and Tatum played worse when impaired.

segments.title: Boyd Raeburn's avant-garde band
segments.summary: Raeburn built a far-out, undanceable band of excellent writers, short-lived but a family to its players.

segments.title: Johnny Richards and his seven-four arrangement
segments.summary: Richards wrote difficult charts, danced seven-four to prove a point, and played bass sax.

segments.title: Frustration, the end of Raeburn, and back to Dorsey
segments.summary: The Raeburn band disbanded in under a year, and he returned to Dorsey for the third time.

segments.title: Where do you live on the road
segments.summary: He explains keeping an apartment in California or New York and living out of a suitcase.

segments.title: Metronome All-Stars 1947 and his first bebop solo on Leap Here
segments.summary: He thinks his solo on Leap Here was his first recorded bebop solo, though he cannot recall the personnel.

segments.title: The Art Tatum of the clarinet and melting into the instrument
segments.summary: Benny Golson heard his records in Philly; he talks about Tatum, Parker and Shaw becoming one with their instruments.

segments.title: Quartet with George Shearing at the Clique, and Bud Powell's resentment
segments.summary: At the Clique club in 1948 the Pettiford All-Stars played, and Powell resented Shearing, even putting thumbtacks on his seat.

segments.title: Selling his alto saxophone to commit to clarinet
segments.summary: He sold his alto in New York so he would never take a doubling job again.

segments.title: Race in bands, and integrated audiences at Minton's
segments.summary: He says musicians cared only about playing; trouble came from outsiders; and Parker's audiences were mixed.

segments.title: Prokofiev, melodic thread and Parker's vibrato
segments.summary: He and Parker shared an interest in Prokofiev; he explains why melody and vibrato matter in Bird's playing.

segments.title: A night with Bird in Hartford, the train and the Salvation Army band
segments.summary: After a Hartford gig he took Parker to a friend Sully's house, rode the train to New York, and later heard Bird play the Salvation Army tune.

segments.title: Charlie Parker skins rabbits
segments.summary: At Sully's house Parker dressed rabbits for hunters, showing how much he knew outside music.

segments.title: Dizzy's role in bebop, and doubts about Miles Davis
segments.summary: He says Dizzy made bebop popular and named it, and rates Miles below Bird and Diz.

segments.title: Twenty Downbeat poll wins and how the All-Stars were picked
segments.summary: He won Best Clarinetist in the Downbeat poll many times; Metronome used critics and musicians.

segments.title: Forming his first big band and the Gerry Mulligan chart that never came
segments.summary: He started a bebop-flavoured dance band and had writers including Lenny Sinisgalli and Mulligan, who showed up late at the first recording.

segments.title: Band members and the Rumpus Room disaster in Memphis
segments.summary: His last big-band job in Memphis ended with Gene Quill's strap stuck in his sax keys on a national broadcast.

segments.title: Listening back: too much arranging and too much clarinet
segments.summary: He says his big-band recordings were over-arranged and overloaded with clarinet, unlike Goodman and Shaw.

segments.title: Metronome All-Stars 1949-50, Stan Getz, and the Miles Davis bootleg
segments.summary: He recalls the 1950 All-Stars with Getz, and a Royal Roost broadcast billing him with Miles.

segments.title: Not listening to himself, CDs, iPods, and classical favourites
segments.summary: He avoids listening to his own records, discusses CDs and headphones, and names Prokofiev, Shostakovich and Ravel.

segments.title: Joining Count Basie's small group and learning economy
segments.summary: In 1950 Basie went small at Willard Alexander's urging, and DeFranco learned economy from him.

segments.title: Personnel of the Basie septet and Willard Alexander
segments.summary: He lists Clark Terry, Wardell Gray, Gus Johnson and Freddie Green, and explains who Willard Alexander was.

segments.title: Basie's modern ear and Clark Terry's nicknames
segments.summary: Basie made the bebop front line work; Clark Terry nicknamed him Buddy DeFrigili.

segments.title: The only white man in Basie's band and the Soundies film
segments.summary: He took static for being the only white member, and a film short had Marshall Royal mime his clarinet solo.

segments.title: Turning down Duke Ellington to run his own big band
segments.summary: Ellington offered him Jimmy Hamilton's chair but he stayed with his own band, a decision he regretted.

segments.title: Manager Lenny Lewis, a brilliant and irritating character
segments.summary: Lewis raised money for the band but clashed with DeFranco and had been chased off by Artie Shaw.

segments.title: How Lenny Lewis raised money and took half the take
segments.summary: Lewis got backers including a wealthy woman and Ross Hastings, and kept half of the income.

segments.title: The disastrous first one-nighter and a riverboat success
segments.summary: The first New Jersey date flopped because the music was undanceable, but a riverboat date for black audiences went over well.

segments.title: Out of Nowhere: a radio hit that never sold
segments.summary: The record got heavy airplay and jukebox plays but MGM said it had not sold.

segments.title: Lenny Lewis cooks the books and disappears
segments.summary: Lewis won the band stands and the library in court and later died alone in a Hollywood motel.

segments.chapter: The Blakey quartet on the road
segments.title: Forming the quartet with Art Blakey at Birdland
segments.summary: The Birdland house band of Blakey, Kenny Drew and Eugene Wright became his touring quartet.

segments.chapter: The Blakey quartet on the road
segments.title: Blakey's intensity and his Muslim name
segments.summary: Blakey got stronger through the night, and he took a Muslim name.

segments.chapter: The Blakey quartet on the road
segments.title: Bookings by Willard Alexander and Billy Shaw, and road manager Milt Gray
segments.summary: He tells how the quartet was booked and how Gray took ham and plates from restaurants.

segments.chapter: The Blakey quartet on the road
segments.title: Blakey drives the station wagon like he plays drums
segments.summary: A story of Blakey driving through a gas station at ninety miles an hour.

segments.chapter: The Blakey quartet on the road
segments.title: Muncie, Indiana: the club owner wants the black players in the cellar
segments.summary: He refused to separate his band, and they stayed together at the band table.

segments.chapter: The Blakey quartet on the road
segments.title: Motel eviction at 3 a.m. and walking out of the Muncie job
segments.summary: The motel ordered the black players out, so the whole group packed up and left for Chicago.

segments.chapter: The Blakey quartet on the road
segments.title: Kenny Drew's admirer and Harry Belafonte's stay in Chicago
segments.summary: He tells of a drunk white fan pursuing Drew and of being threatened after Belafonte stayed in his hotel room, and of Belafonte snubbing him later.

segments.chapter: The Blakey quartet on the road
segments.title: Blakey leaves; Bobby White and Sonny Clark join
segments.summary: Blakey left after about two and a half years to lead his own group; Bobby White and Sonny Clark replaced him.

segments.title: Joining Jazz at the Philharmonic
segments.summary: After first refusing, he accepted Granz's offer with Oscar Peterson, Ray Brown and a drummer behind him.

segments.title: Oscar Peterson and the Gershwin album
segments.summary: Peterson became a lifelong friend and tricked Granz into agreeing to the Gershwin album.

segments.title: Recording with Art Tatum for Norman Granz
segments.summary: He describes the intimidating session with Tatum, who played in odd keys, and the keg of beer.

segments.title: Touring Europe with Dorsey and the Air Force, and Buddy Rich on the plane
segments.summary: Dorsey's band flew with the Air Force; he describes the B17 and Buddy Rich getting sick on a plane ride.

segments.title: Touring with Billie Holiday and the first Monterey festival
segments.summary: He recounts the cold Monterey set with Holiday and Sonny Rollins and her bad Stockholm opening night.

segments.title: Charlie Parker was not crazy
segments.summary: He says Parker was reserved, well spoken and brilliant.

segments.title: Singers: Ella Fitzgerald, Billie Holiday and Sarah Vaughan
segments.summary: He prefers Ella, dislikes singers imitating horns, and says Ella was insecure.

segments.title: Booed in Paris on the 1955 JATP tour
segments.summary: He was booed while playing April in Paris, which he later heard was orchestrated by a critic's trad-jazz fans.

segments.chapter: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
segments.title: Critics: Balliett, Hentoff and the 'cold player' charge
segments.summary: He says critics are necessary and admits his early playing was mechanical.

segments.chapter: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
segments.title: Reichian therapy and warming up his playing
segments.summary: He credits Reichian therapy with freeing him up as a player and speaker.

segments.chapter: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
segments.title: The decline of the clarinet's popularity
segments.summary: He says every instrument has its day and he stuck with the clarinet.

segments.chapter: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
segments.title: Stan Kenton's clinic idea and commissioning Nelson Riddle
segments.summary: With jazz work scarce, he did Leblanc clinics and asked Nelson Riddle for a suite.

segments.chapter: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
segments.title: Cross Country Suite on Dot Records
segments.summary: Riddle's eleven-part suite was recorded for Dot, won a Grammy, and was recently reissued.

segments.chapter: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
segments.title: The bass clarinet album
segments.summary: He prepared for one bass clarinet date, later reissued under Art Blakey's name.

segments.chapter: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
segments.title: A double bill with Bill Haley and the Comets
segments.summary: In Philadelphia he found himself opening for Bill Haley and the Comets.

segments.title: Chosen to lead the Glenn Miller Orchestra
segments.summary: Willard Alexander and Dave McKay picked him to replace Ray McKinley within days.

segments.title: First night with the Miller band and the jazz compromise
segments.summary: He took over mid-concert, leaned on Matt Copus, and fought to play some jazz.

segments.title: Meeting Joyce in Muncie, Indiana
segments.summary: He met his wife Joyce at a concert and she joined the bus.

segments.title: Bus driver Bob Bates and the woman left in Canada
segments.summary: Stories of driver Bob Bates leaving a passenger behind and running over a hitchhiker's suitcase.

segments.title: Burning out after eight years and settling in Panama City
segments.summary: After eight years he crashed, slept for weeks, and moved to Florida.

segments.title: Practice, dental trouble and a break from playing
segments.summary: A jaw problem stopped him playing for months.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: Reading Artie Shaw and Hawking
segments.summary: He reads Shaw's book and books on cosmology.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: The road not taken: psychiatry and Wilhelm Reich
segments.summary: He says he might have gone into psychiatry and talks about Reich.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: Son Chad's sound and lighting work
segments.summary: His son Chad is a sound engineer for festivals.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: Whitefish, Montana and the Buddy DeFranco Jazz Festival
segments.summary: He explains how the Whitefish and Missoula festivals began.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: Meeting Terry Gibbs at Ronnie Scott's
segments.summary: Ronnie Scott had them play together and they formed a group.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: Working with Terry Gibbs and humor on the road
segments.summary: Gibbs led, they recorded often, and humor kept them going.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: Tommy Dorsey's harsh and generous sides
segments.summary: A new Miller recruit quit; Dorsey fired a joking trumpeter but paid DeFranco's hospital bills.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: Artie Shaw's ego and his view of DeFranco's playing
segments.summary: He portrays Shaw as brilliant but dismissive.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: Becoming friends with Shaw late in life
segments.summary: They became friends in California after a San Diego concert.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: The Artie Shaw solos project with Tom Ranier
segments.summary: He tried to isolate Shaw's solos and add new backgrounds.

segments.chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
segments.title: Eddie Daniels, and his students Ronnie Aldrich and Steve Botek
segments.summary: He praises Eddie Daniels and explains why he taught only two people.

segments.summary: His Hannon exercise book and his daily routine.

segments.summary: He lives with tinnitus.

segments.title: Trigger finger, double vision and getting old
segments.summary: He has had trigger finger and double vision.

segments.title: His first clarinet
segments.summary: His father bought a pawnshop clarinet with rent money.

segments.summary: Leonard DeFranco and Louise Giordano, from Foggia and Calabria.

segments.summary: His grandfather's wine, sayings and anticlericalism.

segments.summary: He visited his schizophrenic mother in the hospital.

segments.title: Playing for the musicians in the audience
segments.summary: He plays first for the musicians.

segments.title: Content over commerciality
segments.summary: He sometimes regrets not being commercial.

segments.summary: He thinks jazz is healthy and names Anat Cohen, Paquito D'Rivera and others.

segments.summary: He finds recognition gratifying.
